turn_text: something that I noticed about your office you have a quote right above that door and I'd love to kind of hear your thoughts on it it just says politics is not about ideological purity or moral self-righteousness it's about governing and if a politician cannot compromise he cannot govern effectively so what do you like about that quote and how do you apply it

well it's It's one of the quotes I encourage new members to learn and stuff because politics is the art of the possible. And you got to remember how diverse this country is with different opinions, different religions, different ethnicities, everything else. And we all come to it from our backgrounds that are all different. So we have different opinions. That means our job is to sit down and talk about problems and we all have different solutions and talk about them and bait them. And that means compromising with people that you sometimes disagree with. And that's how you get things done in politics. It's not by insisting on your point of view and not listening to any other point of view. There are some issues that are a matter of principle. How you're going to vote on what you think about abortion is kind of a matter of principle. You're either pro-life or pro-choice or something like that. But 90% of the vote you cast around here are matters of just trying to make government work. As an example, if I'm going to drive, I want to drive 80 miles an hour on the interstate and you only want to go 70, I know let's compromise and we'll have speed limit of 75, something like that. That's just making things work. It's not a matter of principle. So that's what that quote from Henry Clay reminds me of. And I put it above my door so I can read it periodically when I come back and forth and remind myself that I'm not always right. Sometimes you have to listen to other people because sometimes they have ideas too that are worthwhile.

turn_text: So I'd love to hear a bit about what your top priorities have been. during this session of Congress. Can you tell me just a little bit about your priorities for like nationwide priorities and then we can go into more like district specific?

Sure. Yeah, it is. The first thing you have to look at any bill that you look at is good for the nation. Is it good for my state? Is it good for my district? My priorities have been, and they switch over time as different issues come up. Right now, I sit on the Appropriations Committee and trying to get the Appropriations process working again, trying to get the bills approved so that agencies know what their funds are going to be available. and to hold them accountable for the funds that we have given them that they're doing their job as efficiently as they can. And they're only doing what we've authorized them to do and stuff. So that's always been one of the biggest challenges. I've sat on the Appropriations Committee for a couple of decades now. And so we have hearings where we have the oversight of the different agencies that come in. I chair the Interior Subcommittee that has Bureau of Land Management, the Forest Service, all the rest of the Department of Interior, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Geological Survey, the Smithsonian, things like that. It's some pretty exciting programs. But making sure that the appropriations process works has been one of my top priorities. Secondly, I would say that the ag immigration issue is one of the biggest ones that we face right now. The biggest issue facing agriculture is a legal workforce. We have a lot of undocumented workers that have worked here for years and years in the agricultural industry, because frankly, no one else will take the jobs. They actually have to apply to try to get American workers to fill some of these jobs. And there's not American workers that will take a lot of these jobs. So we depend on these foreign workers, if you will. But a lot of them have been here for a number of years. They're undocumented. But they're a part of our society, like anybody else. We need to make this a legal process for them. And with the legislation that we've been looking at, we want them to come out of the woodwork. paid taxes, all that kind of stuff, paid penalty coming here illegally and so forth. But let them participate in society and stuff. So that's, we've got a number of Republicans and Democrats working together to try to pass this bill. We've passed it in the House and the last two Congresses haven't been able to get through the Senate yet, but we're still working on that. But I think if we can address that, it will go a long ways towards solving some of the agricultural problems that we have across the country.

turn_text: Thanks so much. And you talked a little bit about appropriations and the appropriations bill for this year passed about a month ago.
sure that's a relief. Can you tell me just some of the highlights in some of those bills?

Well, for my district, it's obviously important because we do a lot of things to help communities in there, not just with the general programs. As an example, in the interior bill, we make sure that we fully fund PILT, which is payment in lieu of taxes. In states that have a great deal of federal land, we pay for that federal land to counties and school districts as if it were taxable. Now, it doesn't pay as much as if it were on the public tax rolls and stuff, but it reimburses them some for having those public lands within their districts and stuff. If you go to Custer County in Idaho, it's 94% federal land. I mean, they only have 6% actually take out state land. They only have about 2% of their land. They can actually tax. for their school districts, for their county services, for search and rescue, for their hospital, those kind of things. That doesn't give them much of a tax base. So we pay them payment in lieu of taxes to help make up that revenue. We make sure that that's funded in our bill. We make sure that that Indian health services, we've got tribes in Idaho that they have the resources to deliver healthcare to their tribal members. If you look at the energy and water bill, which I used to chair and now the second ranking member on the committee, what we fund at the INL is very important. If you've seen the growth at the Idaho National Laboratory over the last 20 years, a lot of that's been because of the resources we've given them to be able to grow the lab and to do the research that they do in Southeast Idaho. turn_text: Yeah, thank you. And then I know there's quite a bit of community project funding that you secured. Can you tell me a little bit about that and why it's so

There are things called community funding projects that used to be called earmarks, what we changed the name because earmarks got a bad name. I've always been a supporter of those because I think members of Congress know they're district better than anybody else. Now, if you're going to ask for stupid things to be funded, your name is going to be on the front page of the paper. And when people come to us because they go through our committee, some of them, we always ask them, you know, have you thought about what this is going to look like if this gets on the front page of your paper? If we do water and sewer systems in in my bill, well, somebody wants to do water system for say a golf course. People might look at that and go, do we really want to have our taxes being used to do a water system for a golf course that ought to be able to do their own water system, you know, And people think about that and they say, well, maybe that's not a good idea. But when you've got a community, like a rural community in Idaho that needs to improve their water system because they have to meet the clean drinking water standards and the clean water standards and the safe drinking water standards, those are federal laws. So we help them. with the resources necessary to rebuild their water systems to meet those standards because they don't have the resources to do it in a small community. And so a lot of the projects that we help fund or request funding for are to help those smaller rural communities and stuff. I'll give you the example, but I always use Firth Idaho, burn their fire station down accidentally. They've been operating for the last year and a half under their fire station has been operating in an abandoned potato cellar. That's not very good. And so they don't have the resources to rebuild their fire station and replace the fire engine and a few things like that that were damaged. They don't have the tax base to be able to do that. But yet, here's these 1,000 people in Firth and 30,000 people in the surrounding community, depending on the fire department. So we help them with a grant to help them fund rebuilding their fire station and stuff. To me, that's a perfectly legitimate thing. And I think it's important that some of these resources that our taxpayers in Idaho send to the federal government be used back in Idaho. So that's why we ask for these things. We have to list them. If you look at any bill that'll be on the back of the bill on who asked for what. And you can go at our home pages and see what we've requested in community finance projects. And if you think we're doing anything that is stupid, let us know. So far, nobody's called us and told us that.

turn_text: Is there anything else you'd like to share about your work in Washington?

I can tell you that this is, I tell freshmen when they come here, that this will be both the most exciting and frustrating job they've ever had. Because you come here and you think you have an answer for something, and you might have the perfect answer, but you got to convince 218 other people in the house that you're right. And then you got to convince 51 people over in the Senate. Well, the way they're rules are, you got to convince 60 people in the Senate that you're right. Then you got to convince the administration that you're right. And it is a laborious project to get something done. And people will say, well, government shouldn't be that hard to run. I wouldn't want a government that's easy to run. I wouldn't want a government where everybody that has a new idea can just make a law with it and stuff. It ought to go through the rigors of debate and having to convince other members that what you want to do is right. That's okay, but it's frustrating for people out there to go, oh man, you know, why can't Congress ever do anything and that kind of stuff? It's supposed to be hard, and it is. But it is, as I said, the most rewarding job I've ever had being able to represent the people of Idaho.
